podcast.title: Plagiarism Lawsuit for Self-Plagiarism (1985)
podcast.body: John Fogarty, founder and chief songwriter for Credence Clearwater Revival, was sued for plagiarism in 1985 after releasing his solo album "Center Field." The lawsuit alleged that songs on his solo album, specifically "Old Man Down the Road," stole melodies from old CCR songs like "Run Through the Jungle," the copyrights of which were owned by Saul Zaentz of Fantasy Records, not Fogarty himself. "Then, in 1985, John released a solo record called Center Field and it too did very, very well. But then John was served with a lawsuit alleging plagiarism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anti-Government Metaphor
podcast.body: In a 2012 interview with Buds Kappa, Fogarty explained that he used rain as a metaphor for the pervasive government policies around 1969-1970, which he perceived as "baloney" from figures like Richard Nixon regarding the Vietnam War. He described a dichotomy where older generations and the government held one view, and younger people felt quite differently, leading to distrust. "In an interview with Buds Kappa in 2012, Fogarty said, there was the dichotomy of old people saying one thing, and young people feeling quite another thing. And therefore not trusting old people starting with the government, Richard Nixon, in his position on the war."

podcast.title: Contract Dispute and Copyright Transfer
podcast.body: John Fogarty had given ownership of his Credence Clearwater Revival songs to Saul Zaentz, who ran CCR's record label, Fantasy Records, in order to get out of his contract, indicating a strong animosity between them. "Although John had written the songs for Credence, the copyrights, the ownership of the songs he had written, had been given over to a guy named Saul Zance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Courtroom Guitar Demonstration
podcast.body: In his self-plagiarism lawsuit, John Fogarty brought his guitar to court and demonstrated to the judge and jury the differences between his solo song "Old Man Down the Road" and the CCR song "Run Through the Jungle." This demonstration was a key factor in the judge's decision to dismiss the case. "Fortunately, the judge in the case decided not to set a precedent and threw things out, largely because John brought his guitar to court and sat on the stand showing the judge and the jury the differences between the songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Plagiarism Lawsuit Against John Fogarty (1985)
xref.body: Saul Zaentz, who owned the copyrights to Credence Clearwater Revival's songs (including "Run Through the Jungle") through Fantasy Records, sued John Fogarty for plagiarism. Zaentz alleged that Fogarty's solo song "Old Man Down the Road" sounded too similar to "Run Through the Jungle," a song Zaentz owned the copyright to, despite Fogarty having written both. "While in Saul freaked out, got all bent out of shape, and then he sued John for plagiarism, alleging that a song on Center Field called Old Man Down the Road, which John owned, sounded just like an old CCR song called Run Through the Jungle, which Saul owned as the result of the contract dispute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Antagonistic Relationship with John Fogarty
xref.body: There was a lot of loathing between Saul Zaentz and John Fogarty, stemming from Fogarty's decision to give up ownership of his CCR songs to Zaentz to escape his contract with Fantasy Records. "There was a lot of loathing on both sides."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Copyright Ownership Dispute
xref.body: The copyrights to songs written by John Fogarty for Credence Clearwater Revival were transferred to Saul Zaentz, who ran the band's record label, Fantasy Records, as part of a contract dispute settlement. This led to a bizarre lawsuit where Fogarty was sued for plagiarizing himself. "Although John had written the songs for Credence, the copyrights, the ownership of the songs he had written, had been given over to a guy named Saul Zance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Potential for Self-Plagiarism Defense
xref.body: Chad Kroeger is envisioned as potentially needing to defend himself in a similar way to John Fogarty if ever accused of self-plagiarism, due to Nickelback's consistent songwriting formula. "However, should Chief Nickelback, Dude Chad Kruger ever find himself in the same situation as John Fogarty, he'd probably have to defend himself in much the same way."
